Kallosemjen Jewish Cemetery 1

Jewish Cemetery · Kállósemjén, Hungary

Not demolished. The newer of two Jewish cemeteries in Kállósemjén, appearing on an 1872 cadastral map with tombstones through 1941. Jews first settled here in the mid-18th century; the community declared itself Orthodox in 1869 and became a subsidiary of the larger Nagykálló community in 1885, maintaining a synagogue (built in the second half of the 19th century), burial society, mikveh, and Talmud Torah. Nine local Jews died in WWI; in 1918, retreating soldiers joined local residents in looting Jewish shops and homes. By 1944, the Orthodox community numbered 107 under Rabbi Adolf Lőwy of Nagykálló. On April 22, 1944, Hungarian gendarmes confined 94 Jews to a fenced corner lot before transferring them to the Nyíregyháza Ghetto and a holding farm, from which they were deported to Auschwitz in stages starting mid-May. 21 survivors returned; by 1949, only 6 Jews remained in the village.
